{"id": "18:25/q01", "question": "Who states the three hundred and nine year duration?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause continues earlier quoted claims or resumes God's narrative; the variant with 'they said' and the force of 18:26 are disputed.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q01/p1", "position": "God states the sleepers' true duration.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr take the count literally. Al-Ṭabarī says unmarked quotation needs proof; al-Zajjāj calls the number a stronger sign. Al-Baghawī says God's subsequent claim to know best confirms disclosed knowledge. Al-Rāzī cites the intervening ban on dispute; al-Ṭabrisī says an unmarked quotation would leave the proof of divine power incomplete. Ibn Kathīr says the People of the Book gave 300 solar years without the nine and the Ibn Masʿūd report is anomalous with disconnected transmission. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī appeals to passage structure and says their reported figure was 200 or less. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this a possible continuation of the narrative; al-Kuranyolu presents it as interpretation B."}, {"id": "18:25/q01/p2", "position": "The number quotes the People of the Book or other disputants, whose claim God refers back to His own knowledge.", "reasons": "Qatāda connects it to the earlier guesses of 18:22; Maṭar al-Warrāq names Jews, while other accounts name Jews and Christians of Najrān. Ibn Masʿūd's reading inserts 'and they said'; Ibn ʿAbbās and others argue 18:26 would be strange after an exact divine statement. Al-Rāzī and Asad cite the following reply; al-Qāshānī says the duration is not established. Al-Kuranyolu prefers this by verse order and links the sleepers' admission in 18:19. Al-Ālūsī challenges use of 'God knows best' as decisive because it also follows a count Ibn ʿAbbās accepted at 18:22. Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī demand evidence for an unmarked quotation."}, {"id": "18:25/q01/p3", "position": "Some People of the Book said 300 years and others added nine.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Kuranyolu describe variant traditional counts. Al-Khafājī takes the pronoun of 'they added' as the People of the Book; al-Ālūsī finds this weak. Al-Kalbī says Najrān Christians knew 300 but not the extra nine, occasioning revelation of the divine answer."}, {"id": "18:25/q01/p4", "position": "The victorious Cave party stayed hidden for 309 years.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reads the clause as a fresh resumption about the party whose cause prevailed; he links its emergence to Christians overcoming idolatrous Romans in the early fourth century and sees a foreshadowing of Islam's faster victory after the Hijra."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q02", "question": "What interval does their stay in the cave measure?", "turns_on": "Whether the duration belongs to the first sleep, a later interval, the party's concealment, or an allegorical reckoning.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q02/p1", "position": "Their life and sleep from entering the cave until God woke and disclosed them.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī ties this to awakening and discovery in 18:19, 18:21; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī connect the detailed count to the earlier sealed hearing in 18:11. Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers the first interval before awakening and notes Christian historians claimed 240 years. Al-Qurṭubī reports al-Ṭabarī distinguishing this from the unknown period after discovery; Ibn ʿAṭiyya likewise distinguishes the two uses of 'remained'. Mujāhid, as transmitted by al-Suyūṭī, calls 300 plus nine the count of their stay."}, {"id": "18:25/q02/p2", "position": "The count runs from entry until their final deaths.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this as a form of direct divine account, distinct from the awakening endpoint."}, {"id": "18:25/q02/p3", "position": "The known sleep is followed by another, unknown period after discovery or death.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī says 18:26 concerns the span from their souls being taken to the present. Al-Baghawī contrasts the People of the Book's count up to their own era with what only God knows after death. Mujāhid says the later period reached the Qurʾān's revelation; al-Ḍaḥḥāk says until death. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports a proposed reading of 309 years from final death until revelation."}, {"id": "18:25/q02/p4", "position": "The count denotes a hidden party's period before its victory.", "reasons": "Elmalılı connects 309 years with Christian victory over idolatrous Roman rule."}, {"id": "18:25/q02/p5", "position": "The count can mean 25 years plus nine months.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī takes 300 lunar cycles as 25 years and the nine as gestation; he appeals to possible ambiguity in the unit, while al-Ālūsī rejects reducing Quranic years to months as baseless."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q03", "question": "What cave or place is associated with their stay?", "turns_on": "The location reports and archaeological signs do not establish identity conclusively.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q03/p1", "position": "Their cave lay between two mountains.", "reasons": "Mujāhid supplies the physical description."}, {"id": "18:25/q03/p2", "position": "Rujayb near Amman best fits the cave, though identification is unproved.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites Jordanian excavation, archaeological signs and some Muslim reports, and identifies nearby Amman with Roman Philadelphia; he also admits no proposed cave is demonstrably the Qurʾānic cave."}, {"id": "18:25/q03/p3", "position": "Other proposed caves lie at Qāsiyūn, Petra, Scandinavia, or Nakhchivan.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the Scandinavian and Caucasus proposals clash with the Roman setting and reach of Roman power."}, {"id": "18:25/q03/p4", "position": "A Roman cave was shown as the sleepers' site, but its identity is uncertain.", "reasons": "Al-Khwārizmī reports al-Wāthiq sent him to inspect it; he saw hair on displayed bodies, suspected contrivance and possible preservation with aloe or other drying medicines. Al-Qaffāl says Roman identification proves nothing, and al-Rāzī says era and location require unavailable revelation."}, {"id": "18:25/q03/p5", "position": "The cave's exact location cannot be established.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says reason cannot determine it without a revealed text; al-Qaffāl rejects proof from Roman identification. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says none of the proposed sites has decisive evidence."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q04", "question": "When did the sleepers live?", "turns_on": "The reports disagree on dates and the available revelation does not specify them.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q04/p1", "position": "They entered after Jesus, with some disciples still alive.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī infer an early post-Jesus date; al-Qaffāl transmits Ibn Isḥāq's post-Jesus view. Most historians place the episode between Jesus and Muḥammad, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares Christian dates under Decius ending in 425, 437, or 439 CE with shorter Christian estimates."}, {"id": "18:25/q04/p2", "position": "They entered before Jesus and awoke between Jesus and Muhammad.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports this chronology, in which Jesus related their story."}, {"id": "18:25/q04/p3", "position": "They lived before Moses.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports a claim that Moses mentioned them in the Torah, explaining Jewish interest."}, {"id": "18:25/q04/p4", "position": "Their precise era cannot be established.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says reason cannot settle the date, and no revealed text is available; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī observes divergent dates and rulers in transmitted accounts."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q05", "question": "What was the sleepers' physical state during and after the interval?", "turns_on": "Accounts differ about what happened after the awakening.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q05/p1", "position": "They remained alive and asleep throughout the stated cave interval.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī explicitly say alive asleep; al-Nasafī ties it to sealed hearing; Muqātil says colors, hair and clothes were unchanged. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes divine care and awakening after 309 years."}, {"id": "18:25/q05/p2", "position": "They never died and will live until the Resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports this claim from some people."}, {"id": "18:25/q05/p3", "position": "Reports differ on whether they died or slept again after discovery.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī records the divergence; al-Thaʿlabī and the Study Quran explain God's knowledge as concerning the time after death."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q06", "question": "How is the phrase three hundred years read?", "turns_on": "Whether miʾa is nunated, annexed to sinīn, or replaced by a singular or nominative variant; grammarians dispute the plural after a hundred.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q06/p1", "position": "The majority read miʾa with tanwīn, then sinīn separately.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid names Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir; al-Ṭabarī names Medinans, Basrans and some Kufans and prefers it because hundreds usually take singular specifications. Al-Jishumī prefers its Arabic. Al-Wāḥidī and al-Naḥḥās criticize the annexed alternative; ʿUthmān is reported to recite sinīn with nunation. Al-Nashr says all remaining readers pronounce tanwīn, after naming Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf as the readers without it."}, {"id": "18:25/q06/p2", "position": "Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read without tanwīn, annexing miʾa to genitive sinīn.", "reasons": "Other reported readers include Yaḥyā, Ṭalḥa, al-Aʿmash, al-Ḥasan and Khalaf; al-Nasafī also names ʿĀṣim. Abū al-Ḥasan says the plural construction is rare but allowed, Abū ʿAlī adduces poetry, and al-Ālūsī takes the canonical reading itself as Arabic evidence. Abū Ḥātim censured it; al-Samīn rejects that censure. Qirāʾāt ER calls the annexation a tighter unit."}, {"id": "18:25/q06/p3", "position": "Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd have the singular sana after three hundred.", "reasons": "The singular is the usual complement of hundreds; Ibn Masʿūd's codex and Ubayy's reading are both cited."}, {"id": "18:25/q06/p4", "position": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk reads nominativ

{"id": "18:25/q07", "question": "How does sinīn function grammatically?", "turns_on": "The grammatical status of plural sinīn after a hundred and whether it clarifies the count, gives its time unit, modifies it, or belongs to an annexed construction.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q07/p1", "position": "It is an apposition or clarifying substitute for the numbered duration.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash allows substitution for three or hundred with case varying accordingly; Abū Isḥāq calls it appositional emphasis, Abū ʿAlī a substitute for 300, and al-Zamakhsharī explanatory apposition. Al-Wāḥidī lists five parses and prefers an adjectival one; al-Bursawī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reject specification because plural would falsely multiply the count. Al-Ālūsī notes substitution could imply the number was not intended; Abū Ḥayyān objects that Basran grammar disallows some appositional analyses."}, {"id": "18:25/q07/p2", "position": "It is an accusative duration governed by labithū, with the number placed before it.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and al-Naḥḥās also express the underlying order as 'they remained years, three hundred'; Ibn Khalawayh makes sinīn governed by the verb. Al-Wāḥidī prefers this analysis and no pause after 300."}, {"id": "18:25/q07/p3", "position": "It is an accusative specification or explanation of the number.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ cites the verse about forty-two black milch camels; al-Ṭabrisī compares 'ten measures of oil.' Al-Ālūsī reports the objection that plural specification would suggest 900 years, but answers from collective usage. Al-Samīn rejects specification except in poetry, and al-Bursawī calculates 600 or 900 under alternative plural minima."}, {"id": "18:25/q07/p4", "position": "It modifies miʾa as a genitive adjective describing the whole counted group.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq use ʿAntara's poetic plural adjective for forty-two milch camels; al-Wāḥidī prefers this to al-Farrāʾ's explanation. Abū ʿAlī treats the milch-camel term as collective, enabling the adjective to describe the full group."}, {"id": "18:25/q07/p5", "position": "In the annexed reading it is genitive as the complement of miʾa, with plural for singular.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says miʾa has a plural sense; al-Farrāʾ says some Arabs use sinīn for one year. Abū ʿAlī cites poetry with five hundred bows; al-Rāzī cites 18:103, al-Nasafī 18:104. Al-Ālūsī notes its rarity and argues the reading itself establishes usage; al-Wāḥidī reports al-Naẓm's objection."}, {"id": "18:25/q07/p6", "position": "The expression can be supplied as 'three hundred years of years'.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī attributes this implicit construction to al-Farrāʾ, Abū ʿUbayda, al-Kisāʾī and al-Zajjāj."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q08", "question": "Why is the unit 'years' stated after three hundred?", "turns_on": "Whether the explicit plural primarily identifies the unit or adds emphasis.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q08/p1", "position": "It removes uncertainty over whether the three hundred were years, months, days, weeks or hours.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba contrasts bare 300 with measured dirhams. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil say the first revelation gave 300, listeners asked its unit, then Gabriel or revelation supplied 'years and nine more'; al-Wāḥidī notes Ibn Mujāhid permitted a pause after 300 because of the staged descent, but prefers no pause grammatically."}, {"id": "18:25/q08/p2", "position": "The plural can magnify the long duration.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī suggests the plural wording emphasizes the length while remaining appositional."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q09", "question": "What does 'nine' count?", "turns_on": "Whether the established unit carries into the following number, and whose act of adding is described.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q09/p1", "position": "Nine further years.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr explicitly supplies years; al-Zajjāj and al-Qushayrī rule out nights or hours because the prior classifier carries forward, as in 100 dirhams and five. Al-Ṭabrisī, al-Samīn and others identify an omitted noun; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī reject ambiguity after the specified count. Abū al-ʿAbbās uses 2:234 and Arab counting of day-night periods by nights; he says the feminine form excludes months."}, {"id": "18:25/q09/p2", "position": "Its unit is left uncertain or might be months, days or hours.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk is reported to say people did not know the nine's unit, and al-Qāshānī takes it as gestation months; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī argue that the previous years supply the unit."}, {"id": "18:25/q09/p3", "position": "On the quoted-speech reading, the nine is an additional claim by some disputants.", "reasons": "Al-Khafājī assigns 'they added' to the People of the Book, though al-Ālūsī rejects it as weak."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q10", "question": "Why are nine added to the three hundred?", "turns_on": "The notes offer a calendar conversion, an actual extension of sleep, a return to sleep, emphatic wording, or an allegorical monthly unit.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q10/p1", "position": "The extra nine convert 300 solar years into approximately 309 lunar years.", "reasons": "Al-Naqqāsh gives about one lunar year per 33⅓ solar years; Ibn Kathīr and al-Bursawī use roughly three per century. Al-Biqāʿī says 300 follows Jewish reckoning and nine the Arab reckoning. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the two-calendar precision a scientific aspect of inimitability; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī answers arithmetic objections by noting an error of under three months, while al-Bursawī cites al-Kāshifī's 309 years, two months, nine days. Al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī raise astronomical objections; al-Khafājī says a fraction under half a year is rounded."}, {"id": "18:25/q10/p2", "position": "Their sleep genuinely continued nine more years after 300.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī tentatively suggests circumstances prolonged it; al-Ṭībī says they nearly woke at 300 but something kept them asleep. Al-Ālūsī objects that this would require an unexpressed increase in their sleep."}, {"id": "18:25/q10/p3", "position": "They woke briefly and then slept again, adding nine years.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes this to Qatāda and considers it closer than the solar-lunar account."}, {"id": "18:25/q10/p4", "position": "The separate nine emphatically confirms and heightens the long duration.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī compares the confirming exception in Noah's thousand years at 29:14. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the earlier passage minimizes the period while this one stresses 'not merely 300 but nine more'."}, {"id": "18:25/q10/p5", "position": "Nine signifies gestation months after 300 monthly cycles.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says the 300 lunar cycles yield 25 years before waking; al-Ālūsī rejects this allegorical reduction as baseless and contrary to the possible outward duration."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q11", "question": "How is tisʿan pronounced?", "turns_on": "The recorded vowel of the first letter differs.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q11/p1", "position": "The common form has kasra on the tāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī contrasts it with Abū ʿAmr's reported fatḥa; the latter is described as dialectal."}, {"id": "18:25/q11/p2", "position": "Al-Ḥasan and, in one report, Abū ʿAmr open the tāʾ.", "reasons": "The sources compare the pronunciation to ʿashr; al-Ālūsī names the al-Luʾluʾī transmission and calls it dialectal."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q12", "question": "How does azdādū govern 'nine'?", "turns_on": "The syntactic object is agreed in the main parse; the alternative concerns the pronoun's referent.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q12/p1", "position": "'Nine' is its direct object; the underlying noun for additional stay or years is omitted.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī denies an adverbial time parse. {"id": "18:25/q14", "question": "What does the long stay demonstrate?", "turns_on": "The notes offer theological and philosophical explanations of the possibility and significance of extraordinary sleep.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q14/p1", "position": "God can preserve sleepers and raise the dead; the duration is a sign of divine power.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says making the count only a human claim weakens the passage's proof. Al-Rāzī argues from God's power over possibilities and knowledge of particulars; if a day's sleep is possible, so is 300 years. {"id": "18:25/q15", "question": "What report describes attempts to inspect the sleepers?", "turns_on": "The two reports concern different visits and different kinds of evidence.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q15/p1", "position": "Muʿāwiya sought to uncover them; a divinely sent wind burned the men sent in.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī transmits that Muʿāwiya passed the cave on a Roman campaign; Ibn ʿAbbās warned that God had forbidden inspection to someone better than Muʿāwiya, but he sent men anyway."}, {"id": "18:25/q15/p2", "position": "Al-Wāthiq sent al-Khwārizmī to a purported Roman cave; the bodies appeared preserved by human means.", "reasons": "Al-Khwārizmī saw chest hair, suspected a staged display and suggested drying medicines such as aloe; al-Qaffāl says neither the site nor Roman identification is certain."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q16", "question": "How reliable are detailed reports about the cave story?", "turns_on": "Accounts vary widely and no decisive text or physical identification resolves several historical particulars.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q16/p1", "position": "Many transmitted details conflict; the shared core is monotheists fleeing a coercive polytheist king and sleeping in a cave.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī lists reports from al-Qummī, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Ibn Isḥāq, Wahb and al-Nuʿmān; they differ on death, dates, rulers, lineage, looks, names and al-Raqīm. He traces divergence to widespread Christian stories and images, Quraysh's exposure, and Muslim collection of outside traditions through converts. Christian accounts diverge from Muslim reports on number, dog and duration; one Christian chronology names Decius and a fifth-century awakening."}, {"id": "18:25/q16/p2", "position": "Reason and purported site identifications cannot settle the era or location.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī requires an unavailable revealed text; al-Qaffāl says Roman site identification is no proof, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī finds no decisive site evidence."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q17", "question": "Why does the Quran omit many historical details of the sleepers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q17/p1", "position": "It selects what serves guidance rather than giving a complete history.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says names, family, occupations, status, dates, rulers, cities, persecutors and even the dog's identity do not bear on guidance; later historians filled the omissions with divergent reports."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q18", "question": "Is an inward reading of the duration offered?", "turns_on": "The allegories assign nonliteral measures to the years, which al-Ālūsī contests.", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q18/p1", "position": "The numbers can allegorize a 25-year cycle and nine months of gestation.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī reads 300 lunar cycles as 25 years and nine as pregnancy, arguing that the verse leaves the count indefinite; al-Ālūsī condemns this reduction of years to months."}, {"id": "18:25/q18/p2", "position": "Spiritual training may take years directly but only days with a guide.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the allegory and replies that God can guide without intermediaries in hours."}]}
{"id": "18:25/q19", "question": "What does sinīn mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:25/q19/p1", "position": "It means ordinary years.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī glosses the phrase as three hundred years and mentions 30:4."}]}
{"id": "18:28/q01", "question": "What occasion prompted the command to remain with the worshippers?", "turns_on": "The reports differ over Meccan chiefs, later influential converts, and the People of the Bench.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q01/p1", "position": "Quraysh leaders demanded that poor believers be dismissed before they would listen or sit with the Prophet.", "reasons": "Accounts list Bilal, Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab, Salman and Ibn Masud, and mention shabby or smelly clothes and separate meeting times. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan prefer this occasion because the sura is Meccan; Ibn Kathir cites Sad's six companions and Muslim's transmission. Kashshaf compares Noah's opponents (26:111)."}, {"id": "18:28/q01/p2", "position": "Uyayna and al-Aqra, with other influential converts, asked for the poor wool-clad believers to be moved so they could sit near the Prophet.", "reasons": "Salman's report names the pair and poor Muslims including Salman and Abu Dharr. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan say this implies a Medinan setting; Alusi thinks most reports support it. Some reports say the chiefs were not yet Muslim."}, {"id": "18:28/q01/p3", "position": "Uyayna alone requested separation, complaining of Salman's smell and promising elite acceptance.", "reasons": "Muqatil lists Bilal, Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab, Amir ibn Fuhayra, Mihja, Ayman, Abu Hurayra and Ibn Masud, and calls Mihja Badr's first martyr. {"id": "18:28/q02", "question": "Was the verse revealed in Mecca or Medina?", "turns_on": "Which occasion report fits the sura's context.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q02/p1", "position": "It was revealed in Mecca in response to Quraysh.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan favor this from the sura's Meccan setting; Tabatabai says Medinan reports conflict with the passage's context."}, {"id": "18:28/q02/p2", "position": "It was a Medinan exception to the Meccan sura.", "reasons": "Qatada places revelation in Medina; Ibn Abbas and Qatada identify an exception. {"id": "18:28/q03", "question": "How did the Prophet respond to the command?", "turns_on": "The reports describe distinct encounters.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q03/p1", "position": "He found poor worshippers remembering God, sat with them, and praised God for commanding their company in life and death.", "reasons": "Reports vary on whether he found them behind the mosque or in rough clothing, and whether he was first at home. Ibn Kathir notes Tabarani's transmission and Abd al-Rahman ibn Sahl's Companion status."}, {"id": "18:28/q03/p2", "position": "He identified a Quran recitation or reminder gathering as the assembly he had been commanded to stay with.", "reasons": "Reports name a man reciting al-Kahf or al-Hijr, or Abdullah ibn Rawaha reminding companions. Ibn Kathir notes connected and disconnected routes."}, {"id": "18:28/q03/p3", "position": "He urged companions to continue remembrance when they stopped at his arrival, wishing to share the descending mercy.", "reasons": "Thabit transmits this account."}, {"id": "18:28/q03/p4", "position": "He turned from inattentive Umayya and found Salman remembering God.", "reasons": "Al-Rabi says Umayya was distracted while the Prophet spoke."}]}

n turned elsewhere.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata describes patient self, heart and spirit in divine presence; Qashani's stripped poor seek only God."}, {"id": "18:28/q04/p3", "position": "The wording specifies the Prophet's self because his heart was already with God.", "reasons": "Qushayri and Alusi distinguish public conduct from the heart privately reserved for God."}, {"id": "18:28/q04/p4", "position": "For others the phrase hints at the difficulty and merit of company with the poor.", "reasons": "Alusi says this implication applies to others, not to the Prophet; reports urge humility and say such company teaches gratitude and contentment."}]}
{"id": "18:28/q05", "question": "Who are those calling on their Lord?", "turns_on": "Whether the description specifies prayer, broader worship, learning, or the historical companions.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q05/p1", "position": "They are people performing the obligatory prayers, including the five daily and congregational prayers.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Ibrahim, Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas and Kab identify prescribed prayer; Hasan rejects story-preachers in favor of congregational worship. Ibn Kathir says poor or rich, strong or weak may qualify."}, {"id": "18:28/q05/p2", "position": "They perform the dawn and afternoon prayers.", "reasons": "Qatada says prescribed prayers began one year before the emigration."}, {"id": "18:28/q05/p3", "position": "They continually worship and remember God through supplication, praise, glorification, prayer and good works.", "reasons": "Tabari and Ibn Kathir include several acts; Tabarsi says they begin and end each day in worship. Ibn Atiyya includes religious knowledge; Study Quran lists prayer and invocation."}, {"id": "18:28/q05/p4", "position": "They are Quran reciters or pupils whom the Prophet taught to recite.", "reasons": "Abu Jafar says the Prophet taught them; Ubayd Allah names reciters."}, {"id": "18:28/q05/p5", "position": "They discuss distinctions in lawful and unlawful matters.", "reasons": "Abu Hashim and Said ibn Jubayr are cited."}, {"id": "18:28/q05/p6", "position": "They are the poor companions whom elites wanted expelled.", "reasons": "Lists vary, including Salman, Abu Dharr, Suhayb, Ammar, Khabbab, Bilal and Ibn Masud. {"id": "18:28/q06", "question": "What does 'morning and evening' signify?", "turns_on": "Whether the hours are literal, an idiom of continuity, or spiritual symbols.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q06/p1", "position": "It denotes continual devotion across all times.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Abu Hayyan take both ends for the whole; Abu Hayyan likens it to front and back meaning the whole body. Ibn Ashur says prayer spans day and night. Tabatabai calls recurring times a metonym and rejects restriction to named prayers; Study Quran cites 33:42, 48:9 and 76:25."}, {"id": "18:28/q06/p2", "position": "It marks actual morning and evening worship.", "reasons": "Mawardi describes seeking success at morning and pardon at evening; Alusi says work distracts people at these hours and favors the literal times. Ibn Ashur defines morning as dawn to sunrise; Qiraat-Er contrasts a single ghudwa act with ghadat as a period."}, {"id": "18:28/q06/p3", "position": "Waking and sleeping resemble return to life and return to death, inviting remembrance.", "reasons": "Razi says the wise thank God at these transitions."}, {"id": "18:28/q06/p4", "position": "Inwardly, morning and evening signify annihilation and abiding.", "reasons": "Qashani applies the symbols to stripped seekers."}]}
{"id": "18:28/q07", "question": "How is the morning word read?", "turns_on": "The reader transmission, grammar of ghudwa with the article, and value of codex spelling.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q07/p1", "position": "Most readers have bil-ghadati, the standard and grammatically clearer form.", "reasons": "Tabari follows reader consensus; Zajjaj says ghudwa is already definite. Nahhas says written waw proves no pronunciation, comparing salat and hayat. Farisi calls this form clearer."}, {"id": "18:28/q07/p2", "position": "Ibn Amir and some early readers have bil-ghudwati with waw.", "reasons": "Farra attributes it to Abu Abd al-Rahman alone; others add Nasr ibn Asim and Malik ibn Dinar. Defenders generalize or make indefinite the normally definite time word; Alusi compares explanations of Sibawayh, Khalil and Radi. Orthographic waw is disputed."}, {"id": "18:28/q07/p3", "position": "Ibn Abi Abla reads plural morning and evening forms.", "reasons": "Jishumi explains the original waw turning to alif after fatḥa."}, {"id": "18:28/q07/p4", "position": "Abu Abd al-Rahman is reported to read al-ghudu without final h.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya records the variant."}]}
{"id": "18:28/q08", "question": "What do worshippers seek by 'His face'?", "turns_on": "Whether face denotes approval, essence, attributes or vision.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q08/p1", "position": "They seek God's pleasure, favor and approved obedience rather than display, reputation or worldly gain.", "reasons": "Bursevi and Suhayli explain the face metaphor from where approval and anger show or the turn toward one favored; Alusi prefers this. Ibn Ashur says devotion makes them worthy company; Study Quran compares 2:272, 13:22, 30:38-39, 76:9 and 92:18-20."}, {"id": "18:28/q08/p2", "position": "They seek God's essence or nearness by turning to Him.", "reasons": "Alusi reports essence with an omitted genitive and nearness as alternatives; Qashani's stripped seekers seek divine essence without worldly or afterlife needs."}, {"id": "18:28/q08/p3", "position": "God's face means His beautiful names and attributes through which He is addressed.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says the essence cannot be reached directly: seeking active attributes means receiving mercy and grace; seeking knowledge, power and majesty calls for humility, weakness and ignorance. He rejects pleasure, omitted essence and mere nearness."}, {"id": "18:28/q08/p4", "position": "At the highest mystical level it can mean seeking a vision of God.", "reasons": "Study Quran marks this as a highest-level interpretation."}, {"id": "18:28/q08/p5", "position": "They seek God's face through supplication.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi reports supplication as one account of how they seek Him."}, {"id": "18:28/q08/p6", "position": "They seek God's face through their day's work.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi reports that work dedicated to God by day implies even greater devotion at night."}]}
{"id": "18:28/q09", "question": "How does 'seeking His face' function grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q09/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial expression describing their uninterrupted sincere invocation and intention.", "reasons": "Qushayri says devotion persists morning and evening."}]}
{"id": "18:28/q10", "question": "What does 'do not let your eyes pass beyond them' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ada with an simply denotes passing or includes contemptuous recoil.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q10/p1", "position": "Keep attention on poor believers; do not turn the gaze past them toward wealthy people.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says not to pass believers for others. Tabari derives it from surpassing; Razi cites poetry; Tabatabai cites Raghib's root sense of overstepping. Abu Hayyan favors ordinary lexical turning away over semantic incorporation."}, {"id": "18:28/q10/p2", "position": "The wording combines passing over the poor with recoiling from or looking down on them.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari explains ada with an through semantic inclusion of withdrawing or rising above, comparing 4:2; Nasafi says this intensifies the warning. Abu Hayyan objects that Basran grammar licenses inclusion only when necessary. {"id": "18:28/q11", "question": "How is 'do not let your eyes pass' read?", "turns_on": "Verb form, case and number of the eyes, and whether causative morphology changes valency.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q11/p1", "position": "The common reading makes the two eyes the subject.", "reasons": "Farra and Akhfash explain the dual subject; Qurtubi rejects the objection that the verb must govern the eyes directly. Ibn al-Shajari rejects changing the nominative 'your eyes' to the accusative; Zarkashi says the nominative wording still conveys 'do not avert your eye'."}, {"id": "18:28/q11/p2", "position": "Hasan reads a causative form with 'your eyes' accusative.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinni glosses turning the eyes from worldly adornment. Zamakhshari and Lawamih say hamza makes the verb transitive; Abu Hayyan objects that the base is already transitive and should then take two objects."}, {"id": "18:28/q11/p3", "position": "Hasan, Isa and al-Amash are reported with a doubled verb.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari and Abu al-Fadl invoke doubling to explain transitivity, citing al-Nabigha; Abu Hayyan disputes it. A still ayn is also reported from Hasan."}, {"id": "18:28/q11/p4", "position": "A reported variant has the eye singular.", "reasons": "Kashshaf records it with a poetic witness for turning away."}]}

{"id": "18:28/q13", "question": "How is 'desiring worldly adornment' construed?", "turns_on": "Where the circumstance attaches and how singular agreement is explained.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q13/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial present clause describing the possible state of seeking worldly adornment.", "reasons": "The meaning experts, Zamakhshari and Qurtubi take it as hal; Qurtubi cites Imru al-Qays. {"id": "18:28/q14", "question": "What is the worldly adornment toward which the gaze is warned?", "turns_on": "Whether it is general elite company or a specific reported moment.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q14/p1", "position": "It is elite company, status and finery, as contrasted with poor believers' shabby dress.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd calls it the worldly elite. {"id": "18:28/q15", "question": "Does the warning attribute worldly desire to the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether it describes a real motive, missionary concern, or a hypothetical danger.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q15/p1", "position": "It warns about a possible act; the Prophet wanted leaders to believe, not worldly gain.", "reasons": "Wahidi compares 80:5-6; Tabarsi says the Prophet sometimes accommodated leaders for the sake of their followers. {"id": "18:28/q16", "question": "Who is the heedless person whose wishes must not be obeyed?", "turns_on": "Which historical petitioner is named and how far the indefinite wording extends.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q16/p1", "position": "The description originally concerns Quraysh's unbelieving chiefs and extends to anyone with that character.", "reasons": "Tabari and Abu Hayyan see leaders seeking expulsion; Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan favor Quraysh from the Meccan setting. Ibn Ashur stresses indefinite 'whoever' and broad application."}, {"id": "18:28/q16/p2", "position": "It is Uyayna ibn Hisn, sometimes with his father, al-Aqra, or people like him.", "reasons": "Khabbab names Uyayna and al-Aqra; Ibn Abbas in Wahidi names Uyayna and his father. {"id": "18:28/q17", "question": "What is the heedlessness of the heart and what is 'Our remembrance'?", "turns_on": "Whether the term is specified by revelation and faith, neglected duty, or inward attention.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q17/p1", "position": "It is inattentiveness to God, the Quran, faith or monotheism.", "reasons": "Muqatil says Quran; Ibn al-Jawzi names monotheism, Quran and Islam; Mufaddal specifies Quran. Ibn Ashur sees a constitution inattentive to divine unity; Ibn Abbas says the heart was sealed against monotheism."}, {"id": "18:28/q17/p2", "position": "Heedlessness is wasted time, idleness or neglect of duties, while obedience gives the heart life.", "reasons": "Sahl and Qushayri define it through time; Tustari describes a thousand deaths ending in separation and lives ending in meeting the Real, and says sin kills while obedience revives."}, {"id": "18:28/q17/p3", "position": "It is forgetting commanded acts and blessings, following lower desires, or slackness.", "reasons": "Abu Uthman stresses duties and blessings; Ibn al-Jalla stresses slackness; Mawardi reports anything causing heedlessness."}, {"id": "18:28/q17/p4", "position": "It is long hope and preoccupation with gifts or creatures instead of their Giver.", "reasons": "Jawzajani and Mawardi cite long hope; Qushayri contrasts gifts and Giver. {"id": "18:28/q18", "question": "What does 'We made his heart heedless' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether Afala is causative or descriptive and how divine action relates to chosen conduct.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q18/p1", "position": "God caused or created heedlessness in the heart.", "reasons": "Sibawayh calls initial hamza augmentative; Razi argues one cannot intend a particular or undirected heedlessness, so God creates it, and causative Afala is commoner. He answers the waw objection because heedlessness need not immediately cause desire. Sunni authors cite divine creation of acts; Ibn Ashur distinguishes innate disposition from chosen desire. Zarkashi counters Ibn Jinni's coordination argument: following desire need not be a result of being made heedless, since a heedless person need not follow desire."}, {"id": "18:28/q18/p2", "position": "God found the person or heart heedless rather than causing that state.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinni says a causal consequence would use fa rather than waw and cites Afala usage with 2:74, 45:29 and 50:4. Razi transmits Amr ibn Madikarib's poem but prefers causation; Alusi objects that 'finding' suggests new knowledge. Ibn Jinni insists that a resultative following verb would require coordination with fa; he therefore takes aghfalna as 'found heedless'."}, {"id": "18:28/q18/p3", "position": "God left the heart to heedlessness, withdrew support, or did not mark it with faith.", "reasons": "Qaffal proposes worldly gifts, an unmarked heart and leaving it to Satan; Razi says each either still causally implicates God or fails to explain attribution. Rummani compares an unbranded camel or unvowelled book; Alusi calls the account subtle but against the apparent meaning."}, {"id": "18:28/q18/p4", "position": "God exposed the heart to punitive heedlessness after the person's deviation.", "reasons": "Tabarsi compares 61:5; Tabatabai compares coverings and deafness at 18:57 and says punishment follows stubborn opposition without cancelling prior choice."}, {"id": "18:28/q18/p5", "position": "God ascribed or reckoned heedlessness to the person, or found a heart unmarked.", "reasons": "Alusi cites Kumayt's poem for attribution. Kashshaf reports a reading assigning action to the heart; Samin reports Abu al-Baqa's alternative of neglecting remembrance."}]}
{"id": "18:28/q19", "question": "How is 'aghfalna qalbahu' read and parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the heart is accusative object or nominative subject.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q19/p1", "position": "The common reading has God as subject and the heart as accusative object.", "reasons": "Samin identifies na as subject and qalbahu as object; Ibn Atiyya contrasts the alternate nominative reading."}, {"id": "18:28/q19/p2", "position": "A variant opens the lam and raises qalbuhu, making the heart subject.", "reasons": "Reports name Amr ibn Faid, Musa al-Aswari, Amr ibn Ubayd and Abu Mijlaz. {"id": "18:28/q21", "question": "What does 'his affair was furaṭ' mean?", "turns_on": "The root's senses of falling short, going ahead, excess, loss, remorse and moral opposition.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q21/p1", "position": "His affair was wasted, neglected, abandoned or brought to ruin.", "reasons": "Mujahid and Qatada speak of loss; Farra of neglected obedience; Layth of unattended business. Thalabi adds wasted days; Muqatil compares 6:38, and Yahya cites 39:56 and 6:31."}, {"id": "18:28/q21/p2", "position": "His affair exceeded limits through boasting, extravagance or transgression.", "reasons": "Farra and Wahidi connect it with Uyayna's boast of leading Mudar and the Arabs; Ibn Abbas via Ata says he sought rank without piety. {"id": "18:28/q22", "question": "Why must the demand to remove the poor be refused?", "turns_on": "The weight of believers' dignity and the likely outcome of conceding to elites.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q22/p1", "position": "The poor believers' devotion and dignity require their company; social rank does not measure worth.", "reasons": "Bursevi says a person rejecting faith because of poor company is hypocritical, and expulsion violates prophethood; religious leaders attend to inner states. He cites a hadith that God looks at hearts and deeds, a Hafiz couplet, and Abraham's selfless flock gift. Ibn Ashur criticizes elite fixation on appearances."}, {"id": "18:28/q22/p2", "position": "The chiefs' uncertain or outward conversion cannot justify humiliating believers.", "reasons": "Alusi states the objection then answers it: exclusion could alienate hearts, induce apostasy among recent converts and deter future entrants, outweighing a few unbelievers' continued disbelief."}, {"id": "18:28/q22/p3", "position": "The command blocks concessions to polytheists and tells the Prophet to attend to believers.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur calls it a broad rule; Islahi links it to the cave story and sura's opening; Biqai says the cave sleepers foreshadow rescue and elevation over tyrants."}, {"id": "18:28/q22/p4", "position": "Inwardly, do not defer to a veiled person governed by the lower self.", "reasons": "Alusi warns against humbling oneself for wealth, citing a hadith on losing two-thirds of religion; he and a poet describe rich patrons' painful reproach."}]}
{"id": "18:28/q23", "question": "How does this command connect with other verses and its sura?", "turns_on": "How the verse extends 6:52 and fits the surrounding cave passage.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q23/p1", "position": "It strengthens the parallel command at 6:52 not to expel people who call on God.", "reasons": "Razi says 6:52 forbids expulsion while this verse positively commands patient company; Alusi and Ibn Ashur call this more emphatic. {"id": "18:28/q24", "question": "What merits are reported for sitting with worshippers or remembering God?", "turns_on": "The gathering, promised benefit, reported numbers and transmission routes differ.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q24/p1", "position": "Morning remembrance or a preacher's gathering surpasses freeing four slaves; evening remembrance surpasses freeing eight descendants of Ishmael.", "reasons": "Suraqa's report gives dawn to sunrise and four; Anas values eight at twelve thousand each and corrects a four-person version to ninety-six thousand.
